name: Retries and Backoff
intent: Recover from temporary failures by trying again, but wait longer between attempts and add randomness so retries help instead of causing a second outage.
scenario: A database restarts for 2 seconds. 100 app instances all get errors at the same moment and all retry immediately, again and again, so the database is flattened every time it tries to come back.
problem: Many failures are transient: a dropped connection, a brief overload, a failover. Retrying fixes them. But naive retries multiply load on a service that is already struggling, and clients that fail together retry together, creating synchronized waves (a thundering herd) that keep it down.

howItWorks.title: Retry only what is worth retrying
howItWorks.text: Timeouts, connection errors, 503 (service unavailable) and 429 (too many requests) are often temporary. A 400 or 404 will fail again every time, so retrying it is pointless. Only retry operations that are safe to repeat (see idempotency).

howItWorks.title: Wait between attempts, and wait longer each time
howItWorks.text: Exponential backoff doubles the delay after each failure: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms. Early retries are quick for blips, and later ones back off to give a struggling service space. A maximum delay stops it growing without limit.

howItWorks.title: Add jitter so clients do not move in lockstep
howItWorks.text: If every client waits exactly 200 ms, they all return at the same instant. Jitter picks a random delay within the window (for example anywhere from 0 to the backoff). The load spreads out instead of arriving in waves.

howItWorks.title: Cap the attempts and the total time
howItWorks.text: Give up after a few attempts or a deadline, and surface the error. Endless retries hold resources, hide outages and pile up work. If a caller is waiting, the whole retry budget must fit inside its own timeout.

howItWorks.title: Retry at one layer only
howItWorks.text: If three layers each retry 3 times, one user action can become 27 calls. Choose one layer to own retries, and honour Retry-After headers when the server sends them.

pros: Simple to add and very effective against transient faults
With backoff and jitter, recovering clients do not overwhelm the service
Works well with queues and idempotent operations
cons: Without limits, retries amplify load during an outage (a retry storm)
Unsafe for non-idempotent operations: the first attempt may have succeeded
Hard to test, because the interesting behaviour only appears during failures
whenToUse: Calls over a network, where brief failures are normal
Reading from or writing to services that fail over or restart
Message handling where a failed message can be redelivered later
whenNotToUse: Errors that will not change (validation, authorization, not found)
Operations that are not idempotent and have no deduplication
When a circuit breaker is open or the service said to stop (honour that signal)
pitfalls: Retrying immediately in a tight loop
Backoff with no jitter, so clients still retry in synchronized waves
Retries at every layer, which multiplies the traffic
No maximum attempts or deadline, so a failure never surfaces

roles.label: Client
roles.description: Calls the service and decides whether and when to retry.

roles.label: Service
roles.description: The dependency that may fail temporarily.

quiz.question: A client calls an internal service and gets one of four responses. Which one is worth retrying after a short wait, assuming the call is safe to repeat?
options: 400 with a validation error on the request body
401 because the API key is invalid
404 because the order id does not exist
quiz.explanation: A 503 signals a temporary overload, and a Retry-After header may say when to return. The other three will fail the same way every time until the request, key or data changes, so retrying them only adds load.

quiz.question: After a 2-second database restart, 100 app instances use exponential backoff of 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms with no randomness. The database is still overloaded each time it recovers. Which change fixes the pattern?
options: Randomise each delay within the window
Raise the starting delay from 100 ms to 1 s
Add a maximum delay cap of 30 seconds
Allow more attempts before giving up
quiz.explanation: Without jitter every instance retries at the same instants, so the load still arrives in synchronised waves. Random delays spread it out. A longer base delay or a cap shifts the waves in time but they stay in lockstep, and more attempts means more waves.

quiz.question: A gateway, a service and a repository layer each make up to 3 attempts per call. The database starts failing. One user click can reach the database up to 27 times. What is the best fix?
options: Add jitter at every layer to spread the 27 calls
Double the backoff delay in every layer
Lower each layer to 2 attempts and keep all three
Retry in one layer; the others pass errors up
quiz.explanation: Retries multiply across layers, 3 x 3 x 3, so the failing database gets the worst of it. Retrying at one layer keeps the traffic bounded and the retry budget easy to reason about. Jitter and longer delays spread calls out but do not reduce the total, and 2 attempts per layer is still 8.
